title: Olga Limburg Played the Woman Next Door for Fifty Years. Four German States Went Past Her
dek: She was in front of a camera in 1907 and still in front of one in 1957 — aunts, neighbours, housekeepers, forty-nine films. A supporting career is the only kind long enough to be a record of the industry it happened inside, and hers runs straight through the part of German film history that is hardest to write about.
content:
## Fifty years of the woman next door

Olga Limburg was born in Düsseldorf on 5 April 1881 and died in Berlin on 7 March 1970, aged eighty-eight. Her first film role was in 1907. Her last was in 1957. Between 1919 and 1955 she appeared in forty-nine films.

The roles are described, in every account of her, in almost the same words: aunts, neighbours, housekeepers, women next door. Four of her films were opposite Heinz Rühmann, who was the biggest star German cinema had. During those two decades she was one of the busiest actresses in the country.

That is a particular kind of career and it is the kind film history is worst at holding. A lead's filmography is a list of decisions — what to take, what to turn down, when to change. A working supporting actress's filmography is closer to a record of what was being made, because she was in it.

## 1907 to 1957

She came from the theatre and never entirely left it. Her first engagement was in 1901 at the municipal theatre in Poznań; from 1902 she was in Berlin, at the Tribune, the Metropol, the Lustspielhaus, the Komödie, the Theater am Kurfürstendamm. Early on she played supporting parts, and later she moved into what the German accounts call the comical-oldies repertoire — the character parts that come to an actress who has been on a stage for thirty years.

Her film work started in 1907 with a small role in *Fest der Handwerker* and a second in 1910. The silent parts that got her noticed came later: *Prinz Kuckuck* in 1919, *Kean* in 1921, and Rudolf Meinert's *Marie Antoinette, the Love of a King* in 1922. She was in E. A. Dupont's *The Ancient Law* in 1923, and in *The Unknown Tomorrow* the same year, and in *Zigano* and *Dancing Mad* in 1925.

Then sound arrived and she kept working: *Between Night and Dawn* in 1931, two films in 1933, *Victoria in Dover* and *The Girl Irene* in 1936, *Madame Bovary* in 1937, *Napoleon Is to Blame for Everything* and *Five Million Look for an Heir* in 1938, *Hurrah! I'm a Father* in 1939, two more in 1940.

Read that list as a list of years and it does something a career summary cannot. 1919 is the Weimar Republic's first year. 1936 to 1940 is the German film industry under Nazi control. 1954 and 1957, when she made her last two pictures, are the Federal Republic. She was working in all of it.

## The decade the sources go quiet on

Here is the thing I cannot tell you, and would rather say plainly than write around.

The available accounts of Limburg's life record what she appeared in and nothing about what she thought. For the years from 1933 to 1945 that silence is the whole question, and it is not a small one — those are the years in which a German actress's continued employment was itself administered.

I am not going to fill that in. A sentence I invented about her politics would be worth less than the gap, and the gap is at least honest about what the record holds. What can be said is narrow and true: she went on getting cast, in a system where being cast required not being excluded, and the industry that cast her was the one the state had taken over.

That is a real limit on what a filmography can tell you, and it is worth naming on a site that keeps filmographies. A credit is evidence that someone was in a room. It is not evidence of anything else.

## What a supporting career actually holds

The part of her work I would actually go looking for is the 1923 material. *The Ancient Law* — E. A. Dupont's *Das alte Gesetz*, with Henny Porten — opens on Purim in a Galician shtetl in the 1860s, and follows Baruch, a rabbi's son, who plays king Ahasuerus in the Purim spiel, is told actors are respected outside the ghetto, is forbidden to leave, and leaves anyway. He joins a travelling troupe and ends up performing Romeo at an Austrian royal picnic.

It is also one of the Weimar pictures that has genuinely come back. On film scholar Cynthia Walk's initiative the Deutsche Kinemathek restored it digitally, reconstructing the intertitles and scene order from the censorship cards; Philippe Schoeller wrote a new score, the Jakobsplatz Orchestra recorded it, and the restored 135-minute version premiered at the Berlinale on 16 February 2018 with the music played live at the Friedrichstadt-Palast.

Which is the argument for paying attention to actresses like her at all. The films that get restored are chosen for their directors. The people who turn up inside them, over and over, across regimes and formats and decades, were the industry's actual continuity. Nobody writes a retrospective for the woman who played the aunt. She was there for both world wars and the arrival of sound, and she was still there when the pictures started being made in a different country with the same name.

## St. Anne's

She died in Berlin in March 1970. Her ashes were buried at St. Anne's cemetery.

Forty-nine films between 1919 and 1955, and the first credit fifty years before the last. Most of what we have about her is a list of titles and the years beside them. On this site that list is the page — and the years, read in order, are the part that is worth somebody's afternoon.
